1	% Introduction for "Minimum Intervention Reweighting: Adaptive Exponent Selection
2	% for Contamination-Aware Pretraining"
3	% Generated: 2026-05-15
4	% Framing: STABLE (D023 dual-constraint + D029 ESS-only + D035 tau sweep)
5	
6	\section{Introduction}
7	\label{sec:intro}
8	
9	Web pretraining corpora are increasingly contaminated by machine-generated text, with recent estimates placing the synthetic fraction between 20\% and 60\% \citep{cheng2025contamination}.
10	This poses a fundamental threat to model quality: \cite{shumailov2024model} demonstrate that training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible model collapse, and \cite{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger degradation, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
11	As synthetic content becomes ubiquitous, \emph{contamination-aware training}---strategies that explicitly account for data provenance during optimization---is necessary for maintaining pretraining quality.
12	
13	A natural mitigation is detect-and-reweight: assign each sample a weight $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$ based on a detector's estimated synthetic probability $q(x)$, where larger $b$ downweights suspected synthetic text more aggressively \citep{drayson2025detection}.
14	However, the exponent $b$ is a sensitive per-model hyperparameter whose optimal value varies by an order of magnitude across model scales---$b = 1$ for SmolLM-1.7B versus $b = 10$ for GPT-2 124M---and selecting it requires a clean validation set and grid search costing up to $6{\times}$ the base training budget.
15	The practical question is: \emph{given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should $b$ be chosen without validation?}
16	
17	We propose a \emph{dual-constraint framework} that derives the exponent adaptively per batch from two diagnostics computed on the detector scores alone.
18	The effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ measures the weighted fraction of gradient signal from real data and imposes a \emph{quality floor}: $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$---at least enough cleaning.
19	Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ \citep{vehtari2024psis} quantifies weight concentration and imposes a \emph{stability ceiling}: $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$---not so much cleaning that gradient estimates degrade.
20	A key structural insight makes this tractable: $\aeff$ is strictly increasing in $b$ while $\mathrm{ESS}$ is strictly decreasing, so the quality constraint yields a unique lower bound $\btau$ and the stability constraint a unique upper bound $\bess$.
21	We adopt a \emph{minimum intervention principle}:
22	\begin{equation*}
23	  \bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathrm{ESS}(\bstar) \geq \nmin,
24	\end{equation*}
25	the smallest exponent satisfying the quality floor.
26	This is deliberately conservative: apply enough decontamination to meet the quality target, but no more, preserving the largest possible effective sample size.
27	In practice, batches fall into three regimes---already clean ($\bstar{=}0$), quality-binding ($\bstar{=}\btau$), and stability-binding ($\bstar{=}\bess$)---allowing the framework to handle heterogeneous contamination naturally.
28	Unlike the discrete sampling-importance-resampling of \cite{drayson2025detection}, we implement reweighting through direct loss scaling with continuous gradient contributions.
29	
30	We evaluate on continued pretraining of Qwen3-0.6B on 132M FineWeb \citep{penedo2024fineweb} tokens with 40\% synthetic contamination (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
31	Adaptive $\bstar$ with default hyperparameters ($\tau{=}0.8$, $\nmin{=}2$) matches the grid-search-optimal fixed $b$ within seed variance (PPL $17.650 {\pm} 0.007$ vs.\ $17.646 {\pm} 0.007$ across three seeds) at zero validation cost.
32	It outperforms both uniform training (PPL $17.69$) and ESS-only maximum intervention (PPL $17.73$), confirming that minimum intervention is superior to maximum intervention.
33	A lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices for effective reweighting, and the quality threshold $\tau$ admits a wide safe range of $[0.5, 0.8]$ within which all tested values improve over uniform training.
34	
35	Our contributions are:
36	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
37	  \item A dual-constraint framework for adaptive $\bstar$ selection with minimum intervention semantics, providing validation-free per-batch exponent derivation from batch-level diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
38	  \item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-search-optimal performance within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual-constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) (\S\ref{sec:results}).
39	  \item Evidence that a lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector suffices for effective reweighting (\S\ref{sec:results}).
40	\end{enumerate}
41

1	Web corpora increasingly contain machine-generated text.
2	Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
3	Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
4	A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
5	The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.
6	
7	A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
8	\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
9	Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
10	Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
11	Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.
12	
13	Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
14	We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
15	The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
16	The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
17	These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
18	$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
19	$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
20	The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
21	When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.
22	
23	This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
24	Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
25	The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
26	The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.
27	
28	On Qwen3-0.6B continued pretraining with 40\% synthetic contamination (132M+ tokens from FineWeb), adaptive reweighting achieves mean held-out perplexity of 17.651 across three seeds, matching the grid-searched optimum ($b{=}0.5$, mean 17.646) within seed-to-seed variance (\S\ref{sec:results}).
29	The grid sweep requires six complete training runs to identify this optimum; the adaptive method requires one.
30	The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.722---worse than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention degrades training while minimum intervention improves it.
31	A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting.
32	
33	Our contributions:
34	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
35	\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
36	\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-searched best within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
37	\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
38	\end{itemize}

7	\label{sec:related}
8	
9	\paragraph{Synthetic Contamination and Model Collapse.}
10	Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse} \citep{shumailov2024model}.
11	\cite{alemohammad2024mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.
12	More critically, \cite{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction (e.g., $1/1000$) suffices to trigger collapse, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
13	With synthetic content now estimated at 20--60\% of web corpora \citep{cheng2025contamination}, these results motivate contamination-aware training strategies that explicitly account for data provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.
14	
15	\paragraph{Detect and Reweight.}
16	A natural response to contamination is to detect and remove synthetic content.
17	DetectGPT \citep{mitchell2023detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob \citep{shi2024minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal; both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to reweighting frameworks.
18	\cite{feng2025beyond} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples; \cite{guo2025escaping} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
19	Soft reweighting avoids the precision--recall threshold inherent in hard filtering by assigning continuous weights.
20	
21	Most directly related to our work, \cite{drayson2025detection} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is a detector's synthetic probability.
22	We adopt the same weighting formula but differ in several fundamental ways.
23	\textbf{(i)}~Drayson et al.\ select $b$ via validation-set grid search and fix it throughout training; different model scales require different values ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M parameters, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B), making the choice per-model and expensive.
24	Our $\bstar$ is derived per-batch from dual constraints ($\aeff \geq \tau$, $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$) at zero validation cost, following a minimum intervention principle that selects the smallest sufficient exponent.
25	\textbf{(ii)}~Their SIR resampling discretizes the weight distribution; we apply direct loss reweighting with continuous gradient contributions.
26	\textbf{(iii)}~They employ a ModernBERT-150M detector (AUC\,=\,0.986) on WikiText-2 (${\sim}$2M tokens); we show that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices on FineWeb-scale data (132M+ tokens).
27	
28	\paragraph{Data Mixing and Reweighting.}
29	A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
30	At the \emph{domain} level, DoReMi \citep{xie2023doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO with a proxy model, DSIR \citep{xie2023dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, \cite{ye2025mixing} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance, and AIOLI \citep{chen2025aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework.
31	These methods operate at the domain level and do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.
32	At the \emph{instance} level, SoftDedup \citep{he2024softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, and \cite{sow2025dynamic} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees.
33	Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance}---detector scores estimating human vs.\ machine origin---rather than loss, frequency, or domain membership.
34	
35	\paragraph{Theoretical Foundations.}
36	\cite{he2025golden} derive the optimal real-data weight under known mixture proportions, finding the golden-ratio reciprocal (${\approx}0.62$) optimal when both sources are equally sized; their result requires the contamination ratio, unavailable in web-scale settings.
37	\cite{wang2026survive} prove that contaminated recursive training converges at a rate governed by the effective real-data fraction $\alpha$, providing the theoretical motivation for our quality threshold: ensuring $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ guarantees a convergence-rate lower bound.
38	We operationalize this without the known-proportion assumption, estimating $\aeff$ from batch-level statistics online.
39	For the stability constraint, we build on Kish's effective sample size and the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling framework of \cite{vehtari2024psis}.
40	\cite{kimura2024iw} provide a broader treatment of importance weighting under distribution shift, within which our provenance-based reweighting can be viewed as covariate-shift correction where the covariate is synthetic origin probability.
41

43	\noindent\textbf{Summary.}
44	No existing method provides principled per-batch exponent selection without validation.
45	Drayson et al.\ use the same $w{=}(1{-}q)^b$ formula but require per-model grid search; Golden Ratio weighting requires known mixture proportions; DoReMi and DSIR operate at the domain level rather than instance-level contamination.
46	Our dual-constraint framework fills this gap by deriving the minimum intervention $\bstar$ from batch-level diagnostics alone.

4	\paragraph{Training Data.}
5	We sample a 132M-token subset of FineWeb~\citep{penedo_2024_fineweb} as the real-data source.

10	We train a TF-IDF + Logistic Regression classifier on a held-out labeled split, achieving AUC\,=\,0.939 with calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048 after temperature scaling ($T = 0.204$).

The practical question is: \emph{given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should $b$ be chosen without validation?}

We propose a \emph{dual-constraint framework} that derives the exponent adaptively per batch from two diagnostics computed on the detector scores alone.
The effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ measures the weighted fraction of gradient signal from real data and imposes a \emph{quality floor}: $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$---at least enough cleaning.
Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ \citep{vehtari2024psis} quantifies weight concentration and imposes a \emph{stability ceiling}: $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$---not so much cleaning that gradient estimates degrade.
A key structural insight makes this tractable: $\aeff$ is strictly increasing in $b$ while $\mathrm{ESS}$ is strictly decreasing, so the quality constraint yields a unique lower bound $\btau$ and the stability constraint a unique upper bound $\bess$.
We adopt a \emph{minimum intervention principle}:
\begin{equation*}
  \bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathrm{ESS}(\bstar) \geq \nmin,
\end{equation*}
the smallest exponent satisfying the quality floor.
This is deliberately conservative: apply enough decontamination to meet the quality target, but no more, preserving the largest possible effective sample size.
In practice, batches fall into three regimes---already clean ($\bstar{=}0$), quality-binding ($\bstar{=}\btau$), and stability-binding ($\bstar{=}\bess$)---allowing the framework to handle heterogeneous contamination naturally.
Unlike the discrete sampling-importance-resampling of \cite{drayson2025detection}, we implement reweighting through direct loss scaling with continuous gradient contributions.

Recent estimates place the synthetic fraction at 20--60\% of crawled data~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}, and this share grows as language models are deployed for content production at scale.
Training on such contaminated data has concrete consequences: \citet{shumailov_2024_model_collapse} show that recursive training on model outputs leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse}---and \citet{dohmatob_2025_strong_collapse} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger this failure mode, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The remaining 49.9\% of batches have sufficient real-data content to skip reweighting entirely ($\bstar{=}0$).
The per-batch $\bstar$ distribution (median 0.87, mean 1.40) adapts continuously to each batch's contamination composition without any held-out signal.

The grid sweep requires six complete training runs to identify this optimum; the adaptive method requires one.
The ESS-only variant (maximum intervention) yields mean PPL 17.722---worse than the uniform baseline (17.694)---confirming that maximum intervention degrades training while minimum intervention improves it.
A lightweight TF-IDF + Logistic Regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939, calibrated ECE\,=\,0.048) suffices throughout, suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw classification accuracy for provenance-based reweighting.

Our contributions:
\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
\item A dual-constrained framework for adaptive exponent selection: $\bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$, computed per-batch from detector scores with minimum-intervention semantics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
\item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-searched best within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).
\item A demonstration that a lightweight TF-IDF + LR detector with calibrated $q$-scores supports effective reweighting, achieving results comparable to stronger neural detectors (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Problem Setup}
\label{sec:problem-setup}

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}$ denote a pretraining corpus comprising human-written text $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}}$ and machine-generated text $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}$, with unknown contamination rate $\rho = |\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}| / |\mathcal{D}|$.
A pretrained detector assigns each sample a synthetic probability $q(x_i) \in [0, 1]$.
Following \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}, we define per-sample weights
\begin{equation}
  w_b(x_i) = (1 - q(x_i))^b, \quad b \geq 0,
  \label{eq:weight}
\end{equation}
where $b = 0$ recovers uniform weighting and increasing $b$ progressively downweights high-$q$ samples.
The weighted training objective is
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{L}(b) = \frac{\sum_{i} w_b(x_i) \, \ell(x_i; \theta)}{\sum_{j} w_b(x_j)},
  \label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
where $\ell(x_i; \theta)$ is the per-sample language modeling loss.

\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} treat $b$ as a hyperparameter selected via validation-based grid search, with reported optima ranging from $b{=}1$ (SmolLM-1.7B) to $b{=}10$ (GPT-2 124M), making per-model tuning unavoidable.
We instead derive $b$ adaptively per batch from the detector scores alone, requiring no validation set.

\subsection{Dual-Constraint Framework}
\label{sec:dual-constraint}

Higher $b$ removes more synthetic influence but also discards effective training signal.
We formalize this trade-off through two per-batch statistics.

\paragraph{Effective real proportion.}
For a batch $\mathcal{B} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_B\}$ with weights $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^b$, we define
\begin{equation}
  \aeff(b) = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b) \cdot \mathbf{1}[x_i \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}}]}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b)},
  \label{eq:alpha_eff}
\end{equation}
measuring the effective fraction of real data after reweighting.
Since true provenance labels are unavailable at training time, we use the detector's hard prediction $\mathbf{1}[q(x_i) < 0.5]$ as a proxy; all theoretical properties below hold for this approximation.

\paragraph{Effective sample size.}
Kish's effective sample size \citep{vehtari_2024_psis} quantifies weight concentration:
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{ESS}(b) = \frac{\left(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b)\right)^2}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i^2(b)}.
  \label{eq:ess}
\end{equation}
$\mathrm{ESS}(0) = B$ under uniform weights, decreasing toward $1$ as $b \to \infty$ for any batch containing synthetic samples.

\begin{proposition}[Monotonicity]
\label{prop:monotonicity}
For any batch containing both real and synthetic samples with non-identical $q$-scores:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item $\aeff(b)$ is strictly increasing in $b$.
  \item $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ is strictly decreasing in $b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For (1), differentiating Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha_eff} using $\frac{dw_i}{db} = w_i \ln(1 {-} q_i)$ yields
\begin{equation}
  \frac{d\aeff}{db} = \aeff(1 {-} \aeff) \!\left( \mathbb{E}_w[\ln(1{-}q) \mid \mathrm{real}] - \mathbb{E}_w[\ln(1{-}q) \mid \mathrm{synth}] \right)\!,
  \label{eq:dalpha}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{E}_w$ denotes expectation under the normalized weight distribution.
Since real samples have lower $q$-scores, $\ln(1{-}q)$ is strictly less negative for real than synthetic samples, making the parenthesized difference positive.
For (2), increasing $b$ multiplies each weight by $(1{-}q_i)^{\Delta b}$, a factor varying across samples, which concentrates the normalized weight distribution and strictly increases $\sum_i \tilde{w}_i^2$, hence decreasing ESS.
Full proofs appear in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.
\end{proof}

Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity} establishes that quality and sample efficiency move in opposite directions as $b$ increases, motivating two complementary constraints.

\paragraph{Quality lower bound.}
We require $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ for a threshold $\tau \in (0, 1)$.
By strict monotonicity, this defines a unique lower bound
\begin{equation}
  \btau = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}
  \label{eq:b_tau}
\end{equation}
on the exponent---the minimum intervention needed to achieve quality $\tau$.
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} show that pretraining convergence rate scales with effective real data fraction, providing theoretical motivation for maintaining $\aeff$ above a threshold.

\paragraph{Stability upper bound.}
We require $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$ for a floor $\nmin \geq 1$.
By strict monotonicity, this defines a unique upper bound
\begin{equation}
  \bess = \sup\{b \geq 0 : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin\}
  \label{eq:b_ess}
\end{equation}
beyond which gradient estimates become unreliable due to weight concentration.

\paragraph{Minimum intervention principle.}
We select
\begin{equation}
  \bstar = \begin{cases}
    0 & \text{if } \aeff(0) \geq \tau \\
    \btau & \text{if } \btau \leq \bess \\
    \bess & \text{if } \btau > \bess
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:bstar}
\end{equation}
yielding three regimes:
(1)~\textbf{Already clean} ($\aeff(0) \geq \tau$): the unweighted batch meets quality $\tau$; set $\bstar = 0$.
(2)~\textbf{$\aeff$-binding} ($\btau \leq \bess$): the quality constraint determines $\bstar = \btau$, applying the \emph{minimum} intervention to reach $\tau$, with ESS margin remaining.
(3)~\textbf{ESS-binding} ($\btau > \bess$): quality $\tau$ is infeasible under the stability constraint; $\bstar = \bess$ applies the maximum stable intervention.

The key insight is that when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, the method selects its \emph{left} endpoint---downweighting no more than necessary.
This contrasts with an ESS-only strategy that selects $\bess$ (the right endpoint), maximizing cleaning at the cost of discarding useful gradient signal from borderline samples.
In our experiments (\S\ref{sec:results}), 40.1\% of reweighted batches are $\aeff$-binding, where mean $\bstar = 1.67$ compared to $4.15$ under ESS-only---a $2.5\times$ less aggressive exponent that retains $\mathrm{ESS} = 2.60$, well above the floor $\nmin = 2$.

\subsection{Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:solver} solves for $\bstar$ via bisection on $\aeff$, exploiting monotonicity (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity}) to guarantee convergence.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Per-batch adaptive exponent solver}
\label{alg:solver}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Batch scores $\{q_1, \ldots, q_B\}$, threshold $\tau$, ESS floor $\nmin$, tolerance $\varepsilon$, cap $b_{\max}$
\ENSURE Optimal exponent $\bstar$
\IF{$\aeff(0) \geq \tau$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = 0$ \hfill $\triangleright$ Already clean
\ENDIF
\STATE $b_{\mathrm{lo}} \leftarrow 0,\; b_{\mathrm{hi}} \leftarrow b_{\max}$ \hfill $\triangleright$ Bisect for $\btau$
\WHILE{$b_{\mathrm{hi}} - b_{\mathrm{lo}} > \varepsilon$}
  \STATE $b_{\mathrm{mid}} \leftarrow (b_{\mathrm{lo}} + b_{\mathrm{hi}}) / 2$
  \IF{$\aeff(b_{\mathrm{mid}}) < \tau$}
    \STATE $b_{\mathrm{lo}} \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{mid}}$
  \ELSE
    \STATE $b_{\mathrm{hi}} \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{mid}}$
  \ENDIF
\ENDWHILE
\STATE $\btau \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{hi}}$
\IF{$\mathrm{ESS}(\btau) \geq \nmin$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = \btau$ \hfill $\triangleright$ $\aeff$-binding
\ELSE
  \STATE Find $\bess = \sup\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin\}$ via bisection
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = \bess$ \hfill $\triangleright$ ESS-binding
\ENDIF
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Implementation.}
We apply $\bstar$ through loss reweighting: each sample's loss is scaled by its normalized weight $\bar{w}_i = w_{\bstar}(x_i) / \sum_j w_{\bstar}(x_j)$, yielding continuous gradient contributions from all samples including those with intermediate $q$-scores.
This contrasts with the sampling-importance-resampling (SIR) approach of \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}, which discretely resamples a subset of the batch, introducing additional variance and discarding partial information from borderline samples.

\paragraph{Computational cost.}
Each evaluation of $\aeff$ or ESS costs $O(B)$ for batch size $B$.
Bisection requires $O(\log(b_{\max} / \varepsilon))$ iterations, giving total per-batch overhead $O(B \log(b_{\max} / \varepsilon))$---negligible compared to the $O(BHD)$ cost of transformer forward and backward passes with hidden dimension $H$ and depth $D$.
With $b_{\max} = 20$ and $\varepsilon = 0.01$, this amounts to ${\sim}11$ iterations per batch.

\subsection{Hyperparameters}
\label{sec:hyperparameters}

The framework replaces the single sensitive exponent $b$ with two hyperparameters, $\tau$ and $\nmin$, both admitting principled defaults that transfer across settings without per-model tuning.

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} establish that pretraining convergence rate scales with effective real data proportion, motivating a quality threshold.
However, their analysis assumes known mixture proportions; since we do not assume known $\rho$, $\tau$ is an empirical hyperparameter with theoretical motivation rather than a theoretically derived quantity.
We evaluate $\tau \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95\}$ at $\rho = 0.4$ (\S\ref{sec:results}).
All values in $[0.5, 0.8]$ improve over uniform training, with PPL spanning only $0.035$ across this range (17.688 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 17.653 at $\tau{=}0.8$).
We adopt $\tau = 0.8$ as the default.
The sensitivity is asymmetric: under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) yields mild degradation, while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bstar = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$ vs.\ $1.40$ at $\tau{=}0.8$), excessively suppressing borderline samples whose gradient signal remains useful.

\paragraph{ESS floor $\nmin$.}
The stability constraint prevents gradient instability from weight concentration.
At $\nmin = 1$ (effectively unconstrained), $\bstar$ inflates to mean $7.20$ with 46.7\% of batches exceeding $\bstar = 2$, yielding PPL~$= 17.789$---worse than uniform ($17.694$) by $+0.095$, confirming that unconstrained downweighting is harmful.
At $\nmin \geq B$, the constraint forces $\bstar = 0$ for all batches, recovering uniform training.
We use $\nmin = 2$ (half the batch size for $B = 4$), which yields consistent improvement across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).

\paragraph{Comparison with fixed $b$.}
Both $\tau$ and $\nmin$ admit wide effective ranges ($\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$, $\nmin \in \{2, 3\}$) and can be set once without per-model adjustment.
In contrast, the fixed $b$ of \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} spans an order of magnitude across model scales and requires a clean validation set plus grid search costing up to $6{\times}$ the training budget.
Our adaptive $\bstar$ eliminates this cost entirely.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Problem Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

Let $\mathcal{D} = \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}} \cup \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}$ denote a pretraining corpus containing both human-authored and machine-generated text.
The contamination ratio $\rho = |\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}| / |\mathcal{D}|$ is unknown---a realistic assumption for web-scale corpora where synthetic content enters from diverse, uncoordinated sources~\citep{cheng_2025_contamination_survey}.

A pre-trained detector assigns each sample $x$ a synthetic probability $q(x) \in [0,1]$.
Following \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}, we weight each sample as
\begin{equation}
  w(x) = (1 - q(x))^{b},
  \label{eq:weight}
\end{equation}
where $b \geq 0$ controls downweighting intensity: $b = 0$ recovers uniform training, while larger $b$ progressively suppresses high-$q$ samples.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} select $b$ via validation-set grid search, obtaining different optimal values for different model scales ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M parameters, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B).
We instead derive $b$ per-batch from the batch's own $q$-score distribution, requiring no held-out validation data.

\subsection{Dual-Constraint Framework}
\label{sec:dual}

Given a batch $\mathcal{B} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_B\}$ with detector scores $q_i = q(x_i)$ and weights $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^{b}$, we define two batch-level diagnostics that jointly determine $b$.

\paragraph{Effective real proportion.}
Let $r_i = \mathbf{1}[q_i \leq 0.5]$ estimate whether sample $x_i$ is human-authored.
The \emph{effective real proportion}
\begin{equation}
  \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_i(b) \cdot r_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_i(b)}
  \label{eq:alpha}
\end{equation}
measures the share of total weight allocated to likely-real samples.
At $b = 0$, $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ equals the raw real fraction in the batch; increasing $b$ shifts weight toward low-$q$ samples, raising $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.

\paragraph{Effective sample size.}
Kish's effective sample size~\citep{vehtari_2024_psis}
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{ESS}(b) = \frac{\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_i(b)\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{B} w_i(b)^{2}}
  \label{eq:ess}
\end{equation}
quantifies how many equally-weighted samples the weighted batch is equivalent to.
$\mathrm{ESS}(0) = B$; as $b$ grows, a few high-$(1{-}q)$ samples dominate and $\mathrm{ESS}$ drops toward~1.

\paragraph{Monotonicity.}
The two diagnostics exhibit opposing monotonicity in $b$:

\begin{proposition}
\label{prop:monotone}
For any batch containing both real and synthetic samples with distinct $q$-values, $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b)$ is strictly increasing in $b$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $\pi_i(b) = w_i / \sum_j w_j$ denote normalized weights.
Differentiating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} = \sum_i \pi_i r_i$ yields
$\frac{d\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}}{db} = \mathrm{Cov}_{\pi}\!\bigl(r_i,\, \ln(1{-}q_i)\bigr)$.
Real samples ($r_i = 1$) have $q_i \leq 0.5$ and thus higher $\ln(1{-}q_i)$, so this covariance is non-negative for any detector with better-than-random discrimination.
Full derivation in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.
\end{proof}

\noindent $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ is monotonically decreasing in $b$---larger exponents concentrate the weight distribution, a standard property of exponential tilting~\citep{kimura_2024_iw_survey}.

\paragraph{Dual constraints.}
We impose two requirements on $b$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Quality floor}: $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$.
  Convergence under contaminated training improves with the effective real fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}; $\tau$ sets the minimum acceptable quality level.
  By Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}, this constraint defines a \emph{lower bound} $b_\tau = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau\}$.
  \item \textbf{Stability ceiling}: $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$.
  Overly concentrated weights yield high-variance gradients; $n_{\min}$ prevents the batch from degenerating into a single effective sample.
  Since $\mathrm{ESS}$ is decreasing, this defines an \emph{upper bound} $b_{\mathrm{ESS}} = \sup\{b \geq 0 : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}\}$.
\end{enumerate}
The optimal exponent is
\begin{equation}
  b^{*} = \inf\bigl\{b \geq 0 : \alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau\bigr\} \;\;\text{s.t.}\;\; \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}.
  \label{eq:bstar}
\end{equation}
This is the \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the smallest $b$ that achieves the quality floor.
Borderline samples---those with moderate $q$-values---still carry useful training signal; over-downweighting discards this signal unnecessarily.
When both constraints are satisfiable ($b_\tau \leq b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$), $b^{*} = b_\tau$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the binding constraint---$b^{*}$ lies well below the ESS ceiling.
When they conflict ($b_\tau > b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$), the stability ceiling takes precedence: $b^{*} = b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$, accepting a lower $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ to preserve gradient stability.
Figure~\ref{fig:dual_constraint} illustrates the feasible region and the three regimes.

\subsection{Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:bstar} computes $b^{*}$ for each training batch via bisection on the monotone functions $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and $\mathrm{ESS}$.
Each batch falls into one of three regimes:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item \textbf{Clean} ($\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(0) \geq \tau$): the quality floor holds at $b = 0$; no reweighting needed.
  \item \textbf{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding} ($b_\tau \leq b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$): the quality constraint determines $b^{*} = b_\tau$; $\mathrm{ESS}$ remains above $n_{\min}$ with margin.
  \item \textbf{ESS-binding} ($b_\tau > b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$): the stability ceiling caps $b^{*} = b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$.
\end{enumerate}
Across 51{,}913 micro-batches in our main experiment ($\rho{=}0.4$, $\tau{=}0.8$, $n_{\min}{=}2$), 49.9\% are clean, 20.2\% are $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding, and 30.0\% are ESS-binding.
In $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding batches, the solver selects $b^{*} = 1.67$ on average, while an ESS-only strategy would choose $b = 4.15$ on the same batches---2.5$\times$ more aggressive.
The residual $\mathrm{ESS} = 2.60$ in these batches (vs.\ $n_{\min} = 2.0$) confirms that the dual constraint prevents unnecessary over-downweighting.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Per-batch adaptive $b^{*}$ selection}
\label{alg:bstar}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\Require Batch scores $\{q_i\}_{i=1}^{B}$, indicators $\{r_i\}$, quality threshold~$\tau$, ESS floor~$n_{\min}$, search bound~$b_{\max}$, tolerance~$\varepsilon$
\Ensure Optimal exponent $b^{*}$
\If{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(0) \geq \tau$}
  \State \Return $0$ \Comment{clean batch}
\EndIf
\State $b_\tau \gets \Call{Bisect}{\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(\cdot){=}\tau,\; [0, b_{\max}],\; \varepsilon}$
\If{$\mathrm{ESS}(b_\tau) \geq n_{\min}$}
  \State \Return $b_\tau$ \Comment{$\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding}
\Else
  \State $b_{\mathrm{ESS}} \gets \Call{Bisect}{\mathrm{ESS}(\cdot){=}n_{\min},\; [0, b_{\max}],\; \varepsilon}$
  \State \Return $b_{\mathrm{ESS}}$ \Comment{ESS-binding}
\EndIf
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Implementation.}
Given $b^{*}$, we compute normalized weights $\pi_i = w_i(b^{*}) / \sum_j w_j(b^{*})$ and form the weighted loss $\mathcal{L} = \sum_i \pi_i \ell_i$, where $\ell_i$ is the per-sample cross-entropy.
This \emph{loss reweighting} maintains continuous gradients, unlike the SIR resampling of \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} which introduces discrete sampling noise by drawing a subset proportional to $w_i$.
Each bisection requires $\mathcal{O}(B \log(b_{\max}/\varepsilon))$ operations---with $B{=}4$, $b_{\max}{=}20$, and $\varepsilon{=}0.01$, roughly 44 floating-point operations per batch, negligible beside the forward and backward passes.

\subsection{Hyperparameters}
\label{sec:hyperparameters}

The framework introduces two hyperparameters, both with principled defaults set once across all experiments.

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
Convergence theory for contaminated training shows that convergence rate improves with the effective real fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$.
The specific value of $\tau$ is set empirically.
We find a wide safe range: $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ consistently outperforms uniform training (Section~\ref{sec:results}), with $\tau = 0.8$ achieving the best perplexity.
Above 0.8, $b^{*}$ inflates rapidly (mean $b^{*} = 3.08$ at $\tau = 0.95$), causing over-downweighting.
We use $\tau = 0.8$ as the default throughout.

\paragraph{ESS floor $n_{\min}$.}
We set $n_{\min} = 2$ for batch size $B = 4$.
The constraint $n_{\min} < B$ is necessary: $n_{\min} \geq B$ forces $b^{*} = 0$ on every batch, recovering uniform training.
At the other extreme, $n_{\min} = 1$ effectively removes the stability constraint---mean $b^{*}$ rises to 7.20, with 46.7\% of batches hitting the search ceiling at $b_{\max}{=}20$, and perplexity degrades by $+0.14$ relative to $n_{\min} = 2$.
In practice, $n_{\min} \in \{2, 3\}$ yields stable results across seeds (Section~\ref{sec:results}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Synthetic Contamination and Model Collapse.}
Training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible quality degradation---\emph{model collapse} \citep{shumailov2024model}.
\cite{alemohammad2024mad} formalize this as Model Autophagy Disorder, showing that quality or diversity inevitably degrades without fresh real data, even when original training data is retained.
More critically, \cite{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction (e.g., $1/1000$) suffices to trigger collapse, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
With synthetic content now estimated at 20--60\% of web corpora \citep{cheng2025contamination}, these results motivate contamination-aware training strategies that explicitly account for data provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.

\paragraph{Detect and Reweight.}
A natural response to contamination is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT \citep{mitchell2023detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob \citep{shi2024minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal; both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to reweighting frameworks.
\cite{feng2025beyond} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples; \cite{guo2025escaping} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
Soft reweighting avoids the precision--recall threshold inherent in hard filtering by assigning continuous weights.

Most directly related to our work, \cite{drayson2025detection} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is a detector's synthetic probability.
We adopt the same weighting formula but differ in several fundamental ways.
\textbf{(i)}~Drayson et al.\ select $b$ via validation-set grid search and fix it throughout training; different model scales require different values ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M parameters, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B), making the choice per-model and expensive.
Our $\bstar$ is derived per-batch from dual constraints ($\aeff \geq \tau$, $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$) at zero validation cost, following a minimum intervention principle that selects the smallest sufficient exponent.
\textbf{(ii)}~Their SIR resampling discretizes the weight distribution; we apply direct loss reweighting with continuous gradient contributions.
\textbf{(iii)}~They employ a ModernBERT-150M detector (AUC\,=\,0.986) on WikiText-2 (${\sim}$2M tokens); we show that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices on FineWeb-scale data (132M+ tokens).

\paragraph{Data Mixing and Reweighting.}
A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
At the \emph{domain} level, DoReMi \citep{xie2023doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO with a proxy model, DSIR \citep{xie2023dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, \cite{ye2025mixing} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance, and AIOLI \citep{chen2025aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework.
These methods operate at the domain level and do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.
At the \emph{instance} level, SoftDedup \citep{he2024softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, and \cite{sow2025dynamic} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees.
Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance}---detector scores estimating human vs.\ machine origin---rather than loss, frequency, or domain membership.

\paragraph{Theoretical Foundations.}
\cite{he2025golden} derive the optimal real-data weight under known mixture proportions, finding the golden-ratio reciprocal (${\approx}0.62$) optimal when both sources are equally sized; their result requires the contamination ratio, unavailable in web-scale settings.
\cite{wang2026survive} prove that contaminated recursive training converges at a rate governed by the effective real-data fraction $\alpha$, providing the theoretical motivation for our quality threshold: ensuring $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ guarantees a convergence-rate lower bound.
We operationalize this without the known-proportion assumption, estimating $\aeff$ from batch-level statistics online.
For the stability constraint, we build on Kish's effective sample size and the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling framework of \cite{vehtari2024psis}.
\cite{kimura2024iw} provide a broader treatment of importance weighting under distribution shift, within which our provenance-based reweighting can be viewed as covariate-shift correction where the covariate is synthetic origin probability.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Summary.}
No existing method provides principled per-batch exponent selection without validation.
Drayson et al.\ use the same $w{=}(1{-}q)^b$ formula but require per-model grid search; Golden Ratio weighting requires known mixture proportions; DoReMi and DSIR operate at the domain level rather than instance-level contamination.
Our dual-constraint framework fills this gap by deriving the minimum intervention $\bstar$ from batch-level diagnostics alone.

These results motivate \emph{contamination-aware} training strategies that explicitly account for synthetic provenance rather than treating all tokens equally.

\paragraph{Detection and Filtering of Machine-Generated Text.}
Given the severity of contamination, a natural response is to detect and remove synthetic content.
DetectGPT~\citep{mitchell_2023_detectgpt} performs zero-shot detection via probability curvature, while Min-$k$\% Prob~\citep{shi_2024_minkprob} uses the average log-probability of the lowest-$k$\% tokens as a reference-free signal.
Both produce continuous confidence scores suitable as input to downstream weighting---including ours.
On the mitigation side, \citet{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} prove that even an imperfect verifier prevents collapse, but apply hard binary filtering that discards borderline samples.
\citet{guo_2025_escaping_collapse} similarly rely on verification-based selection.
Hard filtering requires a precision--recall threshold; soft reweighting avoids this trade-off by assigning continuous weights.

Most directly related to our work, \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} propose $w_j = (1{-}q_j)^b$ for collapse prevention via detect-and-reweight, where $q_j$ is the detector's synthetic probability.
We adopt the same weighting formula but differ in several fundamental ways.
\textbf{(i)}~Drayson et al.\ select $b$ via validation-set grid search and fix it throughout training; different model scales require different values ($b{=}10$ for ${\leq}360$M, $b{=}1$ for 1.7B), making the choice \emph{per-model} and expensive.
Our $b^*$ is derived per-batch from dual constraints ($\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}} \geq \tau$, $\mathrm{ESS} \geq n_{\min}$) at zero validation cost.
\textbf{(ii)}~Their SIR resampling discretizes the weight distribution; we apply direct loss reweighting with continuous gradients.
\textbf{(iii)}~They employ a ModernBERT-150M detector (AUC\,=\,0.986) on WikiText-2 (${\sim}$2M tokens); we show that a lightweight TF-IDF+LR detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices on FineWeb-scale data (132M+ tokens), suggesting that score calibration matters more than raw detection accuracy.

\paragraph{Data Mixing and Instance-Level Reweighting.}
A parallel line of work optimizes data composition without targeting synthetic contamination.
At the \emph{domain} level, DoReMi~\citep{xie_2023_doremi} learns mixture weights via Group DRO with a proxy model, DSIR~\citep{xie_2023_dsir} performs importance resampling with $n$-gram features, and \citet{ye_2025_data_mixing_laws} discover predictable functional forms relating mixing ratios to performance.
AIOLI~\citep{chen_2025_aioli} unifies these into an online adaptive framework, while \citet{yang_2026_data_mixing_agent} train an RL agent for domain-weight selection.
These methods do not address instance-level contamination within a domain.
At the \emph{instance} level, SoftDedup~\citep{he_2024_softdedup} downweights high-frequency samples via $n$-gram commonness, \citet{sow_2025_dynamic_reweighting} derive sample weights from per-sample loss with convergence guarantees, and \citet{kuo_2024_data_weighting} show that differentiated weighting of LLM-generated data improves downstream classification.
Our reweighting differs from all of these in being driven by \emph{provenance}---detector scores estimating human vs.\ synthetic origin---rather than loss, frequency, or domain membership.

\paragraph{Theoretical Foundations.}
\citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive the optimal real-data weight under known mixture proportions, finding the golden-ratio reciprocal (${\approx}0.62$) optimal when both sources are equally sized.
Their result requires the contamination ratio $k$, unavailable in web-scale settings; we use it as an oracle baseline.
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} prove that contaminated recursive training converges at a rate governed by the effective real-data fraction $\alpha$, providing the theoretical motivation for our quality threshold: ensuring $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ guarantees a convergence-rate lower bound.
We operationalize this without the known-proportion assumption, estimating $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ from batch-level statistics online.
For the stability constraint, we build on Kish's effective sample size and the Pareto-smoothed importance sampling framework of \citet{vehtari_2024_psis}.
\citet{kimura_2024_iw_survey} provide a broader treatment of importance weighting under distribution shift, within which our provenance-based reweighting can be viewed as a special case of covariate-shift correction where the covariate is synthetic origin probability.

\paragraph{Why minimum intervention works.}
The central finding of our experiments is that restraint in downweighting outperforms aggressiveness.
ESS-only reweighting---which maximizes $b$ subject only to $\mathrm{ESS} \geq \nmin$---degrades PPL to 17.723, \emph{worse} than the uniform baseline (17.694, Table~\ref{tab:main}).
The dual-constrained adaptive $\bstar$, by contrast, achieves 17.651 by selecting the \emph{smallest} $b$ that meets the quality floor $\tau$.
The mechanism is clear from the binding statistics: in the 40.1\% of reweighted batches where $\aeff$ binds, mean $\bstar = 1.67$ versus 4.15 under ESS-only---a 2.5$\times$ less aggressive exponent that retains ESS\,=\,2.60, well above the floor $\nmin = 2$.
Over-downweighting discards gradient signal from borderline samples whose detector scores are intermediate (e.g., $q \approx 0.4$--$0.6$); these samples carry partial but non-negligible training value, and aggressively suppressing them impoverishes the effective training distribution.
The $\aeff$ constraint prevents this by halting $b$ as soon as the quality target is met.

\paragraph{$\tau$ as a practical dial.}
The quality threshold $\tau$ controls the trade-off between decontamination strength and sample retention.
Our sweep (Table~\ref{tab:tau}) reveals a wide safe operating range: all $\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$ outperform uniform training, with PPL varying only 0.035 across this interval.
The sensitivity is asymmetric---under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) incurs mild degradation ($-$0.006 to $-$0.015 vs.\ uniform), while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bar{b}^* = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$, 3.08 at $\tau{=}0.95$).
This asymmetry reinforces the minimum intervention intuition: the cost of doing too little is small, whereas the cost of doing too much is steep.
We recommend $\tau = 0.8$ as a principled default; practitioners operating at different contamination rates can adjust within the safe range with low risk.

\paragraph{Connection to convergence theory.}
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} prove that pretraining convergence rate scales with $\alpha$, the effective real data fraction.
Our $\tau$ serves an analogous role---setting a floor on the weighted real proportion per batch---but an important distinction must be noted: their analysis assumes a known contamination proportion, whereas our method estimates quality from detector scores without access to the true $\alpha$.
We therefore position $\tau$ as an empirical hyperparameter with theoretical motivation: convergence theory explains \emph{why} a quality threshold improves training, while the specific value of $\tau$ is determined empirically.
Bridging this gap---deriving $\tau$ from first principles without known proportions---is an open theoretical question.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced Minimum Intervention Reweighting, a dual-constrained framework for contamination-aware pretraining that selects per-batch exponents $b^*$ without validation data.
The method finds the smallest $b$ satisfying $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}(b) \geq \tau$ subject to $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq n_{\min}$, enforcing a minimum-intervention principle: apply only as much downweighting as needed to meet a quality floor, no more.
This stands in direct contrast to ESS-only (maximum-intervention) strategies, which we show degrade performance below even uniform baselines by over-downweighting contaminated samples.

Across three seeds at 0.6B scale with 40\% synthetic contamination, adaptive $b^*$ matches grid-search-optimal PPL (17.651 vs.\ 17.646) within seed variance, eliminating the $|\mathcal{B}|$-run grid search entirely.
The quality threshold $\tau$ is robust across $[0.5, 0.8]$---all values in this range outperform uniform weighting.
A lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,0.94) suffices when post-hoc calibrated (ECE\,0.048); score calibration matters more than raw discriminative power.
The batch-level constraint regime---49.9\% clean (no reweighting needed), 20.2\% $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$-binding, 30.0\% ESS-binding---confirms that both constraints are active and complementary in practice.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Scale.}
All experiments use a single model size (Qwen3-0.6B) with batch size 4.
Batch-level $q$-score statistics concentrate differently at larger batch sizes typical of 3B+ training; the optimal $\tau$ range and constraint dynamics may shift at scale.

\paragraph{Contamination distribution.}
We inject synthetic data via uniform random mixing at a controlled ratio ($\rho{=}0.4$).
Real web-scale contamination is domain-skewed, which may alter within-batch $\alpha_{\mathrm{eff}}$ distributions and require domain-aware extensions.

\paragraph{Detector coverage.}
We evaluate one detector family (TF-IDF + logistic regression).
Although our results suggest calibration dominates discrimination for reweighting quality, a systematic ablation across detector architectures and quality levels is needed.

\paragraph{Threshold.}
$\tau$ is an empirical hyperparameter.
The convergence theory of \citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} assumes a known contamination proportion $\alpha$, which we do not require; bridging this gap to derive $\tau$ from first principles remains open.

\paragraph{Evaluation.}
We report held-out perplexity only.
Downstream task evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag) would strengthen the practical case, particularly at scales where PPL differences translate more reliably to task performance.

\paragraph{Effect size.}
The PPL improvement over uniform weighting is 0.043 at 0.6B/40\% contamination.
While consistent across seeds, this effect is modest; we expect amplification at higher contamination ratios and larger model scales, but verification is ongoing.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Web pretraining corpora are increasingly contaminated by machine-generated text, with recent estimates placing the synthetic fraction between 20\% and 60\% \citep{cheng2025contamination}.
This poses a fundamental threat to model quality: \cite{shumailov2024model} demonstrate that training on recursively generated data leads to irreversible model collapse, and \cite{dohmatob2025strong} prove under scaling-law regimes that even a vanishingly small synthetic fraction suffices to trigger degradation, ruling out data scaling as a remedy.
As synthetic content becomes ubiquitous, \emph{contamination-aware training}---strategies that explicitly account for data provenance during optimization---is necessary for maintaining pretraining quality.

A natural mitigation is detect-and-reweight: assign each sample a weight $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$ based on a detector's estimated synthetic probability $q(x)$, where larger $b$ downweights suspected synthetic text more aggressively \citep{drayson2025detection}.
However, the exponent $b$ is a sensitive per-model hyperparameter whose optimal value varies by an order of magnitude across model scales---$b = 1$ for SmolLM-1.7B versus $b = 10$ for GPT-2 124M---and selecting it requires a clean validation set and grid search costing up to $6{\times}$ the base training budget.
The practical question is: \emph{given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should $b$ be chosen without validation?}

We propose a \emph{dual-constraint framework} that derives the exponent adaptively per batch from two diagnostics computed on the detector scores alone.
The effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ measures the weighted fraction of gradient signal from real data and imposes a \emph{quality floor}: $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$---at least enough cleaning.
Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ \citep{vehtari2024psis} quantifies weight concentration and imposes a \emph{stability ceiling}: $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$---not so much cleaning that gradient estimates degrade.
A key structural insight makes this tractable: $\aeff$ is strictly increasing in $b$ while $\mathrm{ESS}$ is strictly decreasing, so the quality constraint yields a unique lower bound $\btau$ and the stability constraint a unique upper bound $\bess$.
We adopt a \emph{minimum intervention principle}:
\begin{equation*}
  \bstar = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\} \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathrm{ESS}(\bstar) \geq \nmin,
\end{equation*}
the smallest exponent satisfying the quality floor.
This is deliberately conservative: apply enough decontamination to meet the quality target, but no more, preserving the largest possible effective sample size.
In practice, batches fall into three regimes---already clean ($\bstar{=}0$), quality-binding ($\bstar{=}\btau$), and stability-binding ($\bstar{=}\bess$)---allowing the framework to handle heterogeneous contamination naturally.
Unlike the discrete sampling-importance-resampling of \cite{drayson2025detection}, we implement reweighting through direct loss scaling with continuous gradient contributions.

We evaluate on continued pretraining of Qwen3-0.6B on 132M FineWeb \citep{penedo2024fineweb} tokens with 40\% synthetic contamination (\S\ref{sec:experiments}).
Adaptive $\bstar$ with default hyperparameters ($\tau{=}0.8$, $\nmin{=}2$) matches the grid-search-optimal fixed $b$ within seed variance (PPL $17.650 {\pm} 0.007$ vs.\ $17.646 {\pm} 0.007$ across three seeds) at zero validation cost.
It outperforms both uniform training (PPL $17.69$) and ESS-only maximum intervention (PPL $17.73$), confirming that minimum intervention is superior to maximum intervention.
A lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector (AUC\,=\,0.939) suffices for effective reweighting, and the quality threshold $\tau$ admits a wide safe range of $[0.5, 0.8]$ within which all tested values improve over uniform training.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
  \item A dual-constraint framework for adaptive $\bstar$ selection with minimum intervention semantics, providing validation-free per-batch exponent derivation from batch-level diagnostics (\S\ref{sec:method}).
  \item Empirical evidence that adaptive $\bstar$ matches grid-search-optimal performance within seed variance at zero validation cost, and that minimum intervention (dual-constraint) outperforms maximum intervention (ESS-only) (\S\ref{sec:results}).
  \item Evidence that a lightweight TF-IDF + logistic regression detector suffices for effective reweighting (\S\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

A central difficulty is that the contamination proportion in any given corpus is unknown: synthetic text enters through diverse, uncoordinated channels with no centralized provenance record.
The prevalence, severity, and opacity of synthetic contamination make contamination-aware pretraining a practical necessity.

A natural response is \emph{detect-and-reweight}: train a classifier to estimate each sample's synthetic probability $q(x)$, then suppress likely-synthetic samples via the weighting function $w(x) = (1 - q(x))^b$.
\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} demonstrate this approach for model collapse prevention and show that the exponent $b$ critically determines outcomes---their optimal values range from $b{=}10$ for models at ${\leq}360$M parameters to $b{=}1$ at 1.7B, and misspecification degrades results substantially.
Selecting $b$ therefore requires per-model validation-set grid search, with computational cost scaling linearly in the number of candidates (six training runs in a typical sweep).
Other approaches assume even stronger supervision: \citet{he_2025_golden_ratio} derive theoretically optimal weights from convergence analysis but require the exact contamination ratio $\rho$, which is precisely what is unavailable in practice.
Hard detection-and-removal strategies~\citep{feng_2025_beyond_collapse} discard borderline samples entirely, sacrificing the smooth reweighting that continuous $q$-scores enable.

Given per-sample detector scores $q(x)$, how should one choose $b$ without a validation set or known contamination proportion?
We formulate this as a dual-constrained optimization over each training batch: find the smallest $b$ that ensures the weighted effective real proportion $\aeff(b)$ reaches a quality threshold $\tau$, while keeping Kish's effective sample size $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ above a stability floor $\nmin$.
The quality constraint has theoretical grounding: convergence rate under contaminated training improves with the effective real-data fraction~\citep{wang_2026_survive_contamination}, motivating a lower bound on $\aeff$.
The stability constraint prevents extreme weight concentration that degrades gradient quality.
These two requirements exhibit a natural opposition.
$\aeff(b)$ increases monotonically in $b$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotone}), yielding a lower bound $\btau$---the minimum exponent needed to achieve the target quality.
$\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ decreases monotonically, yielding an upper bound $\bess$---the maximum exponent before gradient stability degrades.
The adaptive exponent $\bstar = \btau$ when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, embodying a \emph{minimum intervention principle}: apply the least downweighting sufficient to meet the quality target, preserving as much effective training data as possible.
When the constraints conflict ($\btau > \bess$), the stability ceiling takes precedence.

This minimum-intervention semantics distinguishes the method from the alternative of maximizing $b$ subject only to ESS stability.
Among batches that require reweighting, the dual-constraint solver selects $\bstar$ via the $\aeff$ bound in 40\% of cases, with mean $\bstar{=}1.67$; the ESS-only variant would choose $b{=}4.15$ in these same batches, 2.5$\times$ more aggressive.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Problem Setup}
\label{sec:problem-setup}

Let $\mathcal{D} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}$ denote a pretraining corpus comprising human-written text $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}}$ and machine-generated text $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}$, with unknown contamination rate $\rho = |\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{synth}}| / |\mathcal{D}|$.
A pretrained detector assigns each sample a synthetic probability $q(x_i) \in [0, 1]$.
Following \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}, we define per-sample weights
\begin{equation}
  w_b(x_i) = (1 - q(x_i))^b, \quad b \geq 0,
  \label{eq:weight}
\end{equation}
where $b = 0$ recovers uniform weighting and increasing $b$ progressively downweights high-$q$ samples.
The weighted training objective is
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{L}(b) = \frac{\sum_{i} w_b(x_i) \, \ell(x_i; \theta)}{\sum_{j} w_b(x_j)},
  \label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
where $\ell(x_i; \theta)$ is the per-sample language modeling loss.

\citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} treat $b$ as a hyperparameter selected via validation-based grid search, with reported optima ranging from $b{=}1$ (SmolLM-1.7B) to $b{=}10$ (GPT-2 124M), making per-model tuning unavoidable.
We instead derive $b$ adaptively per batch from the detector scores alone, requiring no validation set.

\subsection{Dual-Constraint Framework}
\label{sec:dual-constraint}

Higher $b$ removes more synthetic influence but also discards effective training signal.
We formalize this trade-off through two per-batch statistics.

\paragraph{Effective real proportion.}
For a batch $\mathcal{B} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_B\}$ with weights $w_i(b) = (1 - q_i)^b$, we define
\begin{equation}
  \aeff(b) = \frac{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b) \cdot \mathbf{1}[x_i \in \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{real}}]}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b)},
  \label{eq:alpha_eff}
\end{equation}
measuring the effective fraction of real data after reweighting.
Since true provenance labels are unavailable at training time, we use the detector's hard prediction $\mathbf{1}[q(x_i) < 0.5]$ as a proxy; all theoretical properties below hold for this approximation.

\paragraph{Effective sample size.}
Kish's effective sample size \citep{vehtari_2024_psis} quantifies weight concentration:
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{ESS}(b) = \frac{\left(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i(b)\right)^2}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{B}} w_i^2(b)}.
  \label{eq:ess}
\end{equation}
$\mathrm{ESS}(0) = B$ under uniform weights, decreasing toward $1$ as $b \to \infty$ for any batch containing synthetic samples.

\begin{proposition}[Monotonicity]
\label{prop:monotonicity}
For any batch containing both real and synthetic samples with non-identical $q$-scores:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item $\aeff(b)$ is strictly increasing in $b$.
  \item $\mathrm{ESS}(b)$ is strictly decreasing in $b$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For (1), differentiating Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha_eff} using $\frac{dw_i}{db} = w_i \ln(1 {-} q_i)$ yields
\begin{equation}
  \frac{d\aeff}{db} = \aeff(1 {-} \aeff) \!\left( \mathbb{E}_w[\ln(1{-}q) \mid \mathrm{real}] - \mathbb{E}_w[\ln(1{-}q) \mid \mathrm{synth}] \right)\!,
  \label{eq:dalpha}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{E}_w$ denotes expectation under the normalized weight distribution.
Since real samples have lower $q$-scores, $\ln(1{-}q)$ is strictly less negative for real than synthetic samples, making the parenthesized difference positive.
For (2), increasing $b$ multiplies each weight by $(1{-}q_i)^{\Delta b}$, a factor varying across samples, which concentrates the normalized weight distribution and strictly increases $\sum_i \tilde{w}_i^2$, hence decreasing ESS.
Full proofs appear in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}.
\end{proof}

Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity} establishes that quality and sample efficiency move in opposite directions as $b$ increases, motivating two complementary constraints.

\paragraph{Quality lower bound.}
We require $\aeff(b) \geq \tau$ for a threshold $\tau \in (0, 1)$.
By strict monotonicity, this defines a unique lower bound
\begin{equation}
  \btau = \inf\{b \geq 0 : \aeff(b) \geq \tau\}
  \label{eq:b_tau}
\end{equation}
on the exponent---the minimum intervention needed to achieve quality $\tau$.
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} show that pretraining convergence rate scales with effective real data fraction, providing theoretical motivation for maintaining $\aeff$ above a threshold.

\paragraph{Stability upper bound.}
We require $\mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin$ for a floor $\nmin \geq 1$.
By strict monotonicity, this defines a unique upper bound
\begin{equation}
  \bess = \sup\{b \geq 0 : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin\}
  \label{eq:b_ess}
\end{equation}
beyond which gradient estimates become unreliable due to weight concentration.

\paragraph{Minimum intervention principle.}
We select
\begin{equation}
  \bstar = \begin{cases}
    0 & \text{if } \aeff(0) \geq \tau \\
    \btau & \text{if } \btau \leq \bess \\
    \bess & \text{if } \btau > \bess
  \end{cases}
  \label{eq:bstar}
\end{equation}
yielding three regimes:
(1)~\textbf{Already clean} ($\aeff(0) \geq \tau$): the unweighted batch meets quality $\tau$; set $\bstar = 0$.
(2)~\textbf{$\aeff$-binding} ($\btau \leq \bess$): the quality constraint determines $\bstar = \btau$, applying the \emph{minimum} intervention to reach $\tau$, with ESS margin remaining.
(3)~\textbf{ESS-binding} ($\btau > \bess$): quality $\tau$ is infeasible under the stability constraint; $\bstar = \bess$ applies the maximum stable intervention.

The key insight is that when the feasible region $[\btau, \bess]$ is non-empty, the method selects its \emph{left} endpoint---downweighting no more than necessary.
This contrasts with an ESS-only strategy that selects $\bess$ (the right endpoint), maximizing cleaning at the cost of discarding useful gradient signal from borderline samples.
In our experiments (\S\ref{sec:results}), 40.1\% of reweighted batches are $\aeff$-binding, where mean $\bstar = 1.67$ compared to $4.15$ under ESS-only---a $2.5\times$ less aggressive exponent that retains $\mathrm{ESS} = 2.60$, well above the floor $\nmin = 2$.

\subsection{Algorithm}
\label{sec:algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:solver} solves for $\bstar$ via bisection on $\aeff$, exploiting monotonicity (Proposition~\ref{prop:monotonicity}) to guarantee convergence.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Per-batch adaptive exponent solver}
\label{alg:solver}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Batch scores $\{q_1, \ldots, q_B\}$, threshold $\tau$, ESS floor $\nmin$, tolerance $\varepsilon$, cap $b_{\max}$
\ENSURE Optimal exponent $\bstar$
\IF{$\aeff(0) \geq \tau$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = 0$ \hfill $\triangleright$ Already clean
\ENDIF
\STATE $b_{\mathrm{lo}} \leftarrow 0,\; b_{\mathrm{hi}} \leftarrow b_{\max}$ \hfill $\triangleright$ Bisect for $\btau$
\WHILE{$b_{\mathrm{hi}} - b_{\mathrm{lo}} > \varepsilon$}
  \STATE $b_{\mathrm{mid}} \leftarrow (b_{\mathrm{lo}} + b_{\mathrm{hi}}) / 2$
  \IF{$\aeff(b_{\mathrm{mid}}) < \tau$}
    \STATE $b_{\mathrm{lo}} \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{mid}}$
  \ELSE
    \STATE $b_{\mathrm{hi}} \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{mid}}$
  \ENDIF
\ENDWHILE
\STATE $\btau \leftarrow b_{\mathrm{hi}}$
\IF{$\mathrm{ESS}(\btau) \geq \nmin$}
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = \btau$ \hfill $\triangleright$ $\aeff$-binding
\ELSE
  \STATE Find $\bess = \sup\{b : \mathrm{ESS}(b) \geq \nmin\}$ via bisection
  \STATE \textbf{return} $\bstar = \bess$ \hfill $\triangleright$ ESS-binding
\ENDIF
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\paragraph{Implementation.}
We apply $\bstar$ through loss reweighting: each sample's loss is scaled by its normalized weight $\bar{w}_i = w_{\bstar}(x_i) / \sum_j w_{\bstar}(x_j)$, yielding continuous gradient contributions from all samples including those with intermediate $q$-scores.
This contrasts with the sampling-importance-resampling (SIR) approach of \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse}, which discretely resamples a subset of the batch, introducing additional variance and discarding partial information from borderline samples.

\paragraph{Computational cost.}
Each evaluation of $\aeff$ or ESS costs $O(B)$ for batch size $B$.
Bisection requires $O(\log(b_{\max} / \varepsilon))$ iterations, giving total per-batch overhead $O(B \log(b_{\max} / \varepsilon))$---negligible compared to the $O(BHD)$ cost of transformer forward and backward passes with hidden dimension $H$ and depth $D$.
With $b_{\max} = 20$ and $\varepsilon = 0.01$, this amounts to ${\sim}11$ iterations per batch.

\subsection{Hyperparameters}
\label{sec:hyperparameters}

The framework replaces the single sensitive exponent $b$ with two hyperparameters, $\tau$ and $\nmin$, both admitting principled defaults that transfer across settings without per-model tuning.

\paragraph{Quality threshold $\tau$.}
\citet{wang_2026_survive_contamination} establish that pretraining convergence rate scales with effective real data proportion, motivating a quality threshold.
However, their analysis assumes known mixture proportions; since we do not assume known $\rho$, $\tau$ is an empirical hyperparameter with theoretical motivation rather than a theoretically derived quantity.
We evaluate $\tau \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95\}$ at $\rho = 0.4$ (\S\ref{sec:results}).
All values in $[0.5, 0.8]$ improve over uniform training, with PPL spanning only $0.035$ across this range (17.688 at $\tau{=}0.5$ to 17.653 at $\tau{=}0.8$).
We adopt $\tau = 0.8$ as the default.
The sensitivity is asymmetric: under-cleaning ($\tau < 0.8$) yields mild degradation, while over-cleaning ($\tau > 0.8$) causes sharper regression as $\bstar$ inflates (mean $\bstar = 2.36$ at $\tau{=}0.9$ vs.\ $1.40$ at $\tau{=}0.8$), excessively suppressing borderline samples whose gradient signal remains useful.

\paragraph{ESS floor $\nmin$.}
The stability constraint prevents gradient instability from weight concentration.
At $\nmin = 1$ (effectively unconstrained), $\bstar$ inflates to mean $7.20$ with 46.7\% of batches exceeding $\bstar = 2$, yielding PPL~$= 17.789$---worse than uniform ($17.694$) by $+0.095$, confirming that unconstrained downweighting is harmful.
At $\nmin \geq B$, the constraint forces $\bstar = 0$ for all batches, recovering uniform training.
We use $\nmin = 2$ (half the batch size for $B = 4$), which yields consistent improvement across three seeds (\S\ref{sec:results}).

\paragraph{Comparison with fixed $b$.}
Both $\tau$ and $\nmin$ admit wide effective ranges ($\tau \in [0.5, 0.8]$, $\nmin \in \{2, 3\}$) and can be set once without per-model adjustment.
In contrast, the fixed $b$ of \citet{drayson_2025_detection_collapse} spans an order of magnitude across model scales and requires a clean validation set plus grid search costing up to $6{\times}$ the training budget.
Our adaptive $\bstar$ eliminates this cost entirely.
